channel.title: TorqueCode — OBD-II Codes, Fixes & Fuel-Saving Tips
channel.description: Plain-language OBD-II code explanations, safe fixes, gear advice and practical fuel-saving tips for drivers and home mechanics.

item.title: Smooth is fast: ease onto the throttle
item.description:
Accelerate with a steady, moderate pedal instead of stabbing it, and brake earlier and more gently. Pretend there is an egg under the pedal that you do not want to crack.

Why it works: Aggressive acceleration and late braking waste kinetic energy and force the engine into its least efficient operating range. Smooth inputs can cut fuel use dramatically in stop-and-go driving.

item.title: Ease off above 50 mph
item.description:
Keep highway speed at or near the limit. A 5 mph reduction above 50 mph can save meaningful fuel on a long commute, and the time difference is usually only a minute or two.

Why it works: Aerodynamic drag rises with the square of speed, so the engine works much harder at 75 mph than at 65 mph. This is one of the largest single fuel levers for highway drivers.

item.title: Kill the long idle
item.description:
Start the car, wait a few seconds for oil pressure, and drive gently. Skip the 10-minute driveway warm-up, and shut the engine off while waiting at long lights, school pickups or drive-throughs where it is safe and legal.

Why it works: An idling engine gets zero miles per gallon while burning roughly 0.2–0.5 gallons per hour. Modern fuel-injected engines warm up faster under light load than at idle.

item.title: Use cruise control on open roads
item.description:
On flat highways and steady-speed roads, let cruise control hold the speed instead of letting your right foot drift. In hilly terrain or heavy traffic, leave it off and drive smoothly by hand.

Why it works: Cruise control avoids the small speed corrections and surges that burn extra fuel. It is most effective on long, constant-speed trips where aerodynamic drag dominates.

item.title: Look two cars ahead
item.description:
Watch traffic far ahead and lift off the throttle early when you see a red light, a stop sign or brake lights. Try to time lights so you roll through them instead of stopping and restarting.

Why it works: Every unnecessary stop turns fuel into brake heat. Anticipating traffic keeps the car moving in its efficient range and reduces wear on the brakes.

item.title: Be smart with A/C and windows
item.description:
At low speeds, open the windows and skip the A/C. At highway speed, close the windows and use A/C on a moderate setting. Use recirculation once the cabin is cool, and park in the shade when you can.

Why it works: Air conditioning can add 10–25% to fuel use in city driving because the compressor loads the engine. At highway speed, the drag from open windows usually costs more than the A/C.

item.title: Shift early, use eco mode
item.description:
In a manual, shift around 1,500–2,500 rpm and stay in the highest comfortable gear. In an automatic, use eco mode if the car has one and let the transmission upshift rather than forcing it to hold a gear.

Why it works: Lower engine speed under light load reduces pumping and friction losses. Eco modes also remap throttle response and shift points to encourage gentler driving.

item.title: Track every fill-up
item.description:
Note the distance and fuel volume at each fill-up, or use a fuel-logging app. Watch the trend rather than a single tank, since weather, traffic and route changes all move the number.

Why it works: A sudden drop in fuel economy is an early warning of low tire pressure, a dragging brake, a failing oxygen sensor or a misfire. Catching it early often turns a breakdown into a cheap repair.

item.title: Check tire pressure monthly
item.description:
Check all four tires when cold, including the spare, and set them to the pressure on the door-jamb label. Do not use the maximum pressure on the tire sidewall as your target.

Why it works: Underinflated tires flex more and create rolling resistance, which the engine must overcome. Properly inflated tires can improve fuel economy by around 3% and last longer.

item.title: Keep the engine breathing
item.description:
Inspect the engine air filter at every oil change and replace it when it is visibly dirty or restricted. Do not over-oil reusable gauze filters, which can contaminate the mass air flow sensor.

Why it works: A severely clogged air filter increases intake restriction and can distort air metering. On modern fuel-injected engines the gain is modest but real, and the filter is inexpensive.

item.title: Use the specified oil viscosity
item.description:
Use the viscosity and specification in your owner's manual, not whatever is on sale. Modern 0W-20 and 0W-16 oils exist to reduce friction; switching to a thicker oil can cost fuel economy.

Why it works: Thinner oils pump more easily and reduce internal friction, especially when cold. The manufacturer's recommendation balances protection and efficiency for your engine.

item.title: Fix misfires and stay on schedule
item.description:
Replace spark plugs at the specified interval and repair any misfire promptly. A flashing check engine light means unburned fuel is reaching the catalyst; stop driving and get it diagnosed.

Why it works: A misfiring cylinder wastes fuel and can destroy a catalytic converter. Even a subtle ignition problem forces the engine to work harder for the same power.

item.title: Fix alignment and dragging brakes
item.description:
If the car pulls, the steering wheel is off-center or the tires wear unevenly, get an alignment. If a wheel feels hot after a drive or the car rolls to a stop unusually quickly, have the brakes checked for drag.

Why it works: Misalignment and dragging brakes add rolling resistance that the engine must constantly overcome. Both also shorten tire and brake life.

item.title: Combine errands into one trip
item.description:
Chain your errands instead of making several separate cold starts. Plan the longest leg last so the engine and cabin are already warm, and walk or bike for very short trips when possible.

Why it works: A cold engine uses extra fuel to warm up and reach closed-loop operation. Several short trips can use noticeably more fuel than one longer trip covering the same distance.

item.title: Route around congestion
item.description:
Check traffic before you leave and take the steady route over the shorter stop-and-go one. On a regular commute, test an earlier or later departure time to avoid peak congestion.

Why it works: Stop-and-go traffic keeps the engine idling and accelerating repeatedly in its least efficient mode. A slightly longer free-flowing route often uses less fuel than a short jammed one.

item.title: Share the ride or combine the school run
item.description:
Carpool, use transit or combine multiple passengers into one vehicle when you can. Even one day a week of shared commuting makes a measurable annual difference.

Why it works: The biggest fuel saving is not driving a second car at all. Sharing a trip halves the per-person fuel use and reduces congestion for everyone else.

item.title: Park in the shade
item.description:
Choose shade or a garage when parking on hot days, and use a windshield sunshade. Vent the hot air with the windows down for the first minute before turning on the A/C.

Why it works: A cooler cabin means the air conditioning compressor has less heat to remove. This is a small but almost effortless saving on hot-weather trips.

item.title: Clear out the excess weight
item.description:
Remove heavy items you do not need: tools, sports gear, cases of water, and anything stored in the trunk or bed for 'someday'. Every 100 pounds matters more in a small car than a large truck.

Why it works: Extra mass must be accelerated and carried, so the engine burns more fuel. Weight hurts city driving most because every stop requires accelerating that mass again.

item.title: Take off the roof rack when unused
item.description:
Remove roof boxes, bike racks and cargo baskets when the trip is over. If you need a rack regularly, choose a low-profile design and keep the box closed and aligned.

Why it works: Roof accessories disturb airflow and can increase highway fuel consumption substantially. The effect grows with speed because aerodynamic drag rises so quickly.

item.title: Choose low-rolling-resistance tires
item.description:
When it is time for new tires, compare rolling-resistance ratings as well as grip, noise and tread life. Pick a tire matched to your climate and driving needs, not just the cheapest option.

Why it works: Tires are responsible for a large share of rolling resistance. Lower-resistance tires can deliver a small but permanent fuel saving over their entire life.

item.title: Tighten the cap and skip the top-off
item.description:
Turn the fuel cap until it clicks, and stop filling at the automatic shutoff. Topping off can force liquid fuel into the EVAP canister and cause a check engine light.

Why it works: A loose cap lets fuel vapor escape and can trigger EVAP codes. Topping off can flood the vapor system, leading to expensive canister repairs and wasted fuel.

item.title: Buy the octane the engine actually needs
item.description:
Use the octane rating in your owner's manual. If regular is recommended, premium buys no extra power or economy. If premium is required, do not cheap out and trigger knock-control retard.

Why it works: Higher-octane fuel resists knock but does not contain more energy. Running premium in a regular-fuel car is mostly an unnecessary expense; running regular in a premium-required car can hurt performance and economy.
